title: No time to lose
hook: Bahiya awakens on the spot, and dies soon after, gored by a cow

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bahiya in the street, and your line, stop at the face. Did you stop at a face and let the story wait? Today, what happened to Bahiya next. Day six hundred fourteen.

Someday I'll call my aunt. Someday I'll start sitting every morning. Someday I'll say sorry for that thing in college. A someday list feels safe because it assumes there's time. Bahiya didn't assume it. When the Buddha told him twice that it wasn't the time, Bahiya's answer was blunt: life is uncertain, yours and mine. He'd come a long way to hear the teaching, and he wasn't willing to wait until after lunch. Yesterday you heard what he was told. Today, how the story ends, and why it ends so fast. Today: no time to lose.
screen: `THE SOMEDAY LIST.` → `LIFE IS UNCERTAIN, YOURS AND MINE.` → `NOT AFTER LUNCH.`

segments.voice: The text says that as he heard those few lines, in the seen only the seen, Bahiya's mind was freed, right there in the street. Then the Buddha went on with his alms round. And not long after, a cow with a young calf attacked Bahiya and killed him. That's the whole of it, in one sentence. On his way back, the Buddha saw the body. He asked the monks to carry it on a litter, to cremate it, and to build a memorial mound for him. When the monks asked what had become of Bahiya, the Buddha said: he was wise; he practiced in line with the teaching; he didn't trouble me with questions about it. He has reached final release. Elsewhere in the canon, in a list of outstanding disciples, Bahiya is named foremost among those who understood quickly. Sit with the shape of the story for a moment. A man traveled far, asked three times, heard a few lines, understood them, and died soon after. If he had waited for the right time, there would have been no time. The early texts have a word for this kind of alertness: appamada, heedfulness, not letting things slide. It doesn't mean panic. Bahiya wasn't frantic; he was clear. It means the good thing you can do today is today's.
screen: `FREED, RIGHT THERE IN THE STREET.` · `A COW WITH A YOUNG CALF.` · `FOREMOST IN QUICK UNDERSTANDING.` · `IF HE HAD WAITED.` · then, large: `NO TIME TO LOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't delay the good. Sit and settle. Let your someday list come to mind, and look for one item on it that's small: a message, a thank you, an apology, a few minutes of sitting. Pick that one. Picture yourself doing it today, where and when. Then let it go and rest with the breath, knowing it's waiting for you. Calm, not hurried. The bell holds the time.
Appamada, heedfulness. Bahiya asked to be taught at once, because life is uncertain; he understood at once, and died soon after. Today's word.
Your line: today is today's. Take the one small good thing off your someday list and do it before the evening. Day six hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes tell Bahiya's story to illustrate appamada, heedfulness, and Theravada tradition, following the canon's list, remembers him as the disciple foremost in quick understanding.

fork.setup: you're a monk with the Buddha. you find Bahiya's body by the road, killed by a cow. what does the Buddha ask you to do?
options: leave it; he wasn't ordained yet.
carry it, cremate it, and build a memorial mound.
fork.reveal: he asks for full honor: a litter, cremation and a mound. then he tells the monks Bahiya has reached final release.

original.note: Pali appamada: heedfulness, diligence, not letting things slide.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story is a sad accident.
what it means: it's a story of timing: Bahiya asked at once because life is uncertain, and there turned out to be just enough time.
what a scholar hears: the Udana ends Bahiya's story with the verse on where earth, water, fire and air find no footing, and AN 1 names him etadagga, foremost, in quick understanding.
recall: a monk who had been a wandering poet

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1, Etadagga Vagga (Bahiya foremost in quick understanding)

notes: Udana 1.10 paraphrased. Confirm 'a cow with a young calf', the Buddha's instructions for cremation and a stupa, and his description of Bahiya.
Confirm Bahiya's place in AN 1 as foremost of those of quick understanding (khippabhinna).

The text says Bahiya was not yet ordained (the commentary says he was looking for a bowl and robes); this is left out of the voice but is in the fork option as a distractor; confirm the fork wording is fair.
